item.title: Money, taste, dealflow, hustle, trust
item.description:
Published on July 30, 2026 3:00 PM GMT

Lately, I’ve been thinking a lot about the design of grant programs, from small microgrants to regranting to ambitious new platforms to galaxy-brained schemes for impact markets. Here are five components that I think any grant program needs to be good:

1. Money

This one is obvious: a grant program needs money to give out.

Historically in EA and AI safety, this started as individual small donations from earning-to-give, to Dustin Moskovitz’s money via Good Ventures, to an ill-fated boom around the FTX Future Fund, and now everyone preparing for the frothy Anthropic and OpenAI dollars.

2. Taste

This is also kind of obvious. Most people’s image of “what makes a good grantmaker” is “excellent taste”, which is to say, the ability to discern between good or bad projects.

Grant taste comes in a few forms:

  • Taste in people: founders of projects, leaders of orgs
  • Taste in ideas: whether a particular idea might succeed; whether it’d be good if it did
  • Taste in fields: cause prio across technical AI safety vs policy vs fieldbuilding

One problem with taste is that everyone invariably thinks that they have good taste. Also, there isn’t necessarily One True Taste, so it can be a bit confusing to think about “better” or “worse” taste. Money might instead consider whether one particular Taste is aligned with her values.

How do you improve your taste? Probably: doing similar work yourself; seeing many examples; getting feedback from peers or a mentor; watching grant results over time.

3. Dealflow

“Dealflow” is a term of art among startup investors, to refer to the funding opportunities (”deals”) that come across your table.

Good dealflow can look like:

  • Seeing projects that other funders wouldn’t
  • Seeing many more projects than other funders
  • Good opportunities contact you first, or preferentially accept your funding
  • Creating opportunities from scratch

“Improving dealflow” currently feels underrated among philanthropic funders. Compare the shenanigans VCs pull to generate dealflow (sponsor events, host podcasts, post thinkpieces, ask for intros), versus what EA funders do (…put up an RFP?).

Ways to improve dealflow include: reach outside your existing scene; invest into comms and marketing; offer a good grantee experience for retention + referrals; provide value beyond just Money (such as connections, advice, intros); share dealflow between other funders; chase hard on great founders.

4. Hustle

“Hustle” is my catch-all term for the legwork that goes into coordinating between money, taste, and dealflow; it also covers the logistics that go into getting the grants to the grantees. People with money or taste are often incredibly time-poor; hustle is the glue that keeps the grant program together.

The word hustle may conjure an image of some shady car salesman hustling to sell you a piece of junk. But hustle doesn’t have to look like that. It’s often a polite follow up, being relentless about moving the ball forward, in a way that your counterparties would endorse.

It doesn’t even have to come from a human; you could automate hustle with infrastructure that reduces the number of human touchpoints required, as we do on Manifund via digital grant agreements and self-serve payouts over Stripe Connect.

I think hustle is also currently quite underrated. Parts of EA & AI safety feel like a competition to demonstrate the highest IQ, or write the best-argued blog post — a culture inherited from academic norms. There’s a lot of room for generalists to contribute, by coordinating well and moving money quickly.

5. Trust

Trust, like hustle, is more of a meta component. If the different components above don’t trust each other, no grants will be made.

Ben Kuhn identifies trust as a bottleneck to growing teams quickly; across AI safety philanthropy, I expect trust will likewise be the bottleneck to deploy this wave of funding. The AI safety community has started with a lot of mutual trust due to being small, weird, demanding, and socially interwoven; this probably won’t scale.

Oli Habryka has spoken about the “cursed game of philanthropy”: the lack of trust behind the principal (Money) and agent (Taste) in any kind of philanthropic system. They’re designing Lightcone Commons to require less trust, by placing final funding decisions in the hands of money; I’m interested in seeing how that plays out.

Another way to resolve the trust bottleneck is to colocate Money and Taste in a single person. Leo Gao’s microgrants, giving out his own money from OpenAI, is one currently operating example. I’m excited for the Anthropic and OpenAI windfalls to empower more employees, and hope that they don’t just delegate it all away to funds. I like AI safety regranting because it likewise colocates Money with Taste or Dealflow, to individuals with a strong track record in AI safety nonprofits.

I’m also interested in other ways of increasing trust across the funding ecosystem. Manifund’s commitment to transparency is one way we push for more trust; we’d love to see other funders ask applicants to publish their project proposals, and in turn publish how much money they grant. Other ways to foster trust include in-person events and hubs; social vouching; writeups, retros, reasoning transparency, shared mental models; establishing track records of taste.

Breaking down some recent grant programs

ACX Grants

  • Money: Mostly from well-monied patrons who are ACX readers; about a quarter from Scott directly.
  • Taste: Scott Alexander, now increasingly via judges he recruits to help review proposals
  • Dealflow: ACX readers
  • Hustle: Scott sending a zillion emails and generally coordinating everything himself. (More recently, Manifund helping with payout logistics)
  • Trust: Banked up in Scott over twenty years of blogging

grantmaking.ai

  • Money: Anton Makiiesvkyi put up $1m of his own money from earning to give
  • Taste: Delegated to Manifund regrantors Gavin Leech, Marcus Abramovitch, and Ryan Kidd
  • Dealflow: launched on LessWrong/EA Forum/Manifund/AISafety.com
  • Hustle: Matt Brooks built the site, Melissa Samworth designed it, lots of legwork by Anton
  • Trust: The team having collaborated for a while

Lightcone Commons

  • Money: Jaan, Dustin, a mix of smaller donors and funds
  • Taste: Evaluators like Zvi, Eliezer, Nate Soares et al
  • Dealflow: a launch announcement, maybe more marketing to come?
  • Hustle: Oli & the Lightcone team
  • Trust: Banked up in Oli, having succeeded at various projects like LessWrong and Lighthaven, and more topically Lightspeed Grants and SFF

Coefficient Giving

  • Money: Mostly via Dustin/Good Ventures, but now soliciting external donors
  • Taste: a small army of specialized grantmakers across different sub-funds
  • Dealflow: mix of RFPs and active grantmaking. Because they have a lot of money, basically all big orgs seek them out.
  • Hustle: another army of ops/logistics people
  • Trust: Originally inherited via Givewell, now stands as an institution in itself

 

Can money buy taste/dealflow/hustle/trust?

In some ways, yes:

  • You can offer grantmakers a high salary and get better talent. (But beware principal-agent problems.)
  • If you’re known to have a lot of money, the deals will come to you (for better or for worse). You can also buy dealflow via paid referrals and advertising.
  • You can likewise hire people with hustle, or pay to develop systems that automate grant logistics
  • You can design incentive systems that encourage trust between actors, eg Taste a % cut of Money granted. (Yes, this might incentivize recommending more $; no system is perfect.)

But also, it’s sometimes hard or expensive or suboptimal to directly convert money into things you want. There’s a lot of alpha in finding shortcuts.

So: if you have money, and want to give it away: think about what components you have and need. If there’s someone you trust with taste, dealflow, and hustle, you could simply hire them to do it.

If you have moderate trust in someone else’s taste and want to outsource the dealflow and hustle, come talk to us — this is what Manifund specializes in!

 

Appendix

Title inspired by Holden Karnofsky’s Rowing, Steering, Anchoring, Equity, Mutiny

I also love these reflections from new grantmakers:

  • Scott Alexander, So You Want To Run A Microgrants Program
  • Linch Zhang, Some unfun lessons I learned as a junior grantmaker
  • Joel Becker, Some fun lessons I learned as a junior regrantor
  • Zach Stein-Perlman, Some things I noticed while LARPing as a grantmaker

item.title: Community Polls on Alignment Controversies II
item.description:
Published on July 30, 2026 8:25 PM GMT

Please spend <5 minutes filling in the below polls on AI alignment!

Thank you to everyone who filled out last month's polls. It was great to see 60+ comments engaging with these issues.

This month’s survey has already been taken by a panel of 15 alignment researchers, including Scott Alexander (ACX), David Manheim (ALTER), Jeff Sebo (NYU), and Tobias Baumann (CRS). We'll compare panel and community responses in an upcoming report, which we'll publish here and on LessWrong. To get notified when it's released, you can subscribe to our new Substack.

Many people we've talked to have very different intuitions about where the alignment community stands on the below issues. We hope that your responses to these polls, and the resulting report, will help map core areas of (dis)agreement within the field, and ground CaML's research agenda.

A few final things about the polls themselves:

  • Timeframe: unless a statement says otherwise (e.g. post-AGI), read forward-looking claims as being about roughly the next 2 years.
  • We're not trying to find the 'right' answers. Please answer based on your own best guess.
  • % agree is your % credence in a given position
  • Please let us know if you think the questions are ambiguous or embed false assumptions
  • Any further engagement with the content of the polls in the comments is encouraged

item.title: When you donate can matter more than where
item.description:
Published on July 31, 2026 5:05 PM GMT

And why our 2023 regrant to Timaeus was goated

We think the for-profit funding ecosystem has some cool properties. Different funders naturally come in at different stages, from angel investors who are good at spotting early opportunities to large funds who might invest in late-stage startups to public market traders. Funders race to back promising projects. And the more they get right, the more they’re rewarded with more money to invest in the future.

It would be great if more of those properties existed in nonprofit funding as well. We think that the flow from “person makes great early donation” → “person has more influence” is too weak. And as opposed to the VC world, where investors compete against each other to invest in something quickly, nonprofit funding is beset by “funder chicken,” in which a funder waits for other funders to fill an opportunity, each trying to preserve their capital. This makes fundraising a slog.

What if donating to nonprofits worked more like investing in companies? Impact markets have been talked about in EA for a while. At Manifund, we dream of bringing impact markets to the AI safety funding ecosystem. And at the very least, we want to import more for-profit norms.

What does this look like concretely?

Timaeus: a case study in charitable ROI

Timaeus started as a planned 6-month research project on developmental interpretability, and got its first funding in August 2023, getting $143k from Manifund regrantors. They announced their launch in October 2023. Later in the fall, they got a $455,000 grant from SFF.

In 2024, they continued to get funding from Manifund and SFF, and in 2025 they got two larger grants of $2m and $1.5m from Coefficient Giving. Then in June of this year, they announced that they were merging into Resolution, which got $160m from Coefficient Giving — their largest AI safety grant to date.

What if Timaeus had been a startup? Their early investors would have earned extraordinary returns. It’s unclear how much of Resolution’s funding to credit to Timaeus; looking at the founding team, it looks to be roughly half from Timaeus and half from UK AISI. But okay, maybe Geoffrey Irving specifically gets a lot of the credit here. Even conservatively allocating 20% to Timaeus, if you compare a total of $599,700 raised in 2023 to $160m * 20% = $32m in 2026, you get a 53x return.

(Two key assumptions: all donations in a single year are treated as one funding round, and the amount of impact equity sold is constant year over year.)

Multiplied out, our $143k stake via our 2023 regrants would have grown 53x to now be worth $7.6m. This first regrant to Timaeus, alone, would more than pay back the entire Manifund regranting budget to date ($5.2m). Since the Resolution grant is so much larger than most other AIS grants, Timaeus could be the single best 2023 AI safety grant in these terms.

In an impact-market world, our regrantors might have cashed out during the Resolution merger, and reinvested proceeds to fund more early projects.

Donate early, donate fast

What lessons can you take from the VC world for your own donations?

In the for-profit world, investing in early-stage startups is high-risk, but that’s where the highest-return investments come from. Similarly, we think the best donations come from someone with good taste spotting early opportunities.

You can also have a high impact just by getting grants out the door quickly; good seed investors will say yes after one call rather than get beaten to the punch. AI 2040 predicts that the foremost AI company will have 3 months of lead time when they fully automate AI R&D. So helping an AI safety project start 3 months earlier is really valuable!

(This is why we love regranting. Jesse Hoogland, the founder of Timaeus, affirmed that “getting early support from Manifund made a real difference for us. This was the first funding we received for research and meant that we could start months earlier than we otherwise would have.”)

Finally, consider looking at who has made the best returns on their grants when considering where to direct your donations. It’s easy to look at a fund’s track record and think “oh hey they donated to MATS, I like MATS, I’ll support that fund.” We like MATS too! But donation timing can matter a lot more than the donation target. In retrospect, the first donation to MATS was worth orders of magnitude more than a marginal donation to them today.

item.title: Urban Animals Deserve a Global Nonprofit
item.description:
Published on August 2, 2026 7:08 PM GMT

TLDR

Most urban animals, especially those other than cats and dogs, are highly neglected, even though probably tens of billions of them live in urban environments, and suffer from preventable harms. This post argues for a global nonprofit that would research the problem, test interventions and support local groups under the idea that cities are multispecies societies.

Despite major uncertainty about scale and expected value, this could directly help many urban animals and potentially have strong flow through effects: urban animals could serve as a bridge for empathy toward all animals, support wild animal welfare research, and bring new people and funding into the movement.

In my view, a nonprofit dedicated specifically to urban animal welfare, compared with programs run by organizations with a broader focus that work on animals both in nature and in cities, could better address the distinct challenges of urban environments, avoid some of the philosophical controversy surrounding interventions in nature, and attract more funding and people, including from outside the traditional animal advocacy movement.

Thanks to @Ben Stevenson,  @Max Taylor,  Richard Parr and Noa Deutsch for helpful comments on this post. All mistakes are my own.

Epistemic Status

Very unsure about the numbers I present and the real impact of interventions. I may well be missing important arguments, both for and against this idea. But I am pretty sure there should be at least one global non-profit working solely for urban animals; that part seems quite robust to me.

What are Urban Animals

Urban animals, sometimes described as liminal animals, are free animals living in human dominated environments, like pigeons, mice, lizards, hedgehogs, cats, insects and so on. The space of urban animal welfare can also include wild animals passing through urban areas, e.g. migrating birds, or animals living alternately between the urban and the wild, like jackals and boars.

Urban animals sit in the middle of the human domination spectrum; they are not confined like farmed animals, but not living in an evolutionarily designed environment like wild animals. They live in an environment very accurately crafted, but not for them😔. Humanity doesn't recognize that we live in a multi-species society, hence animals' interests are a neglected or nonexistent part of city planning, infrastructure, and architecture.

What do Urban Animals Suffer From? 

If we think about stray cats, most of them die very young, starve to death, suffer from disease, get hit by cars, lack safe spaces from heat and cold, and more. The infrastructure in the city, the food leftovers, and human behavior are not tuned to their welfare. The same causes of suffering (with some exceptions) also apply to pigeons, mice, rats, lizards and many other urban animals. Like wild animals, most urban animals don't have any "services" to help them; they are akin to living in a collapsed state, with no social or security services. 

Some examples: 
Like urban cats, most pigeons are born into short, fragile lives: in one urban colony study, roughly 45% of baby pigeons died within their first month after leaving the nest (Hetmański 2007), with the main cause of death being hunger. In some cases there are surprisingly easy solutions for reducing the suffering of urban animals, like egg swapping, replacing eggs with dummies to reduce pigeon reproduction.

The urban environment is a dangerous place for animals, and poisoning is one such danger: Rethink Priorities estimates, with high uncertainty, that about 31 million rodents in U.S. urban areas are exposed to rodenticides each year, and rodenticide poisoning can cause days of intense suffering before death.

Animals passing through the city can also be helped; more than a billion birds, many of whom are migrating, die annually in the US alone from building collisions, and terrestrial wild animals get hit by cars.

Neglectedness

Urban animals seem like an effective group to work on from a macro perspective because they are very neglected (not including cats and dogs). The space doesn't even have a clear well recognized name. Animals like mice, pigeons and reptiles living in urban areas are especially overlooked. A globally minded non-profit that tries to systematically change their lives on a macro scale, combining knowledge from experts in architecture, biology, and politics, is nowhere to be found, as far as I know.

Even for cats and dogs, for whom local initiatives are numerous, I didn't find an effective macro level organization that tries to tackle systematic issues, e.g. a technical solution to prevent cats from entering the engines of cars.

Most neglected is the global, cross city, evidence first layer. Existing urban animal work is often local, fragmented, emergency driven, or species siloed. There is activity, but it is usually focused on cats and dogs and not on systematic solutions.

Organizations Whose Work Includes Neglected Urban Animal Species

  • Wild Animal Initiative funds many urban animal welfare research projects. This list includes more than 80 research projects it has funded, many of which relate to urban animals and show that the line between urban animals and wild animals is not always clear
  • The Center for Wild Animal Welfare works to help wild animals, including those in urban areas, by promoting bird safe glass, fertility control (instead of painful poisons) for mice and rats, and much more
  • Sentience, "invisible animals" campaign. An effective-altruism-style push focused specifically on urban pigeons and rats, demanding humane pigeon lofts and a rodenticide phase-out (see related EA Forum post on interventions to improve pigeons’ welfare)
  • The NYU Wild Animal Welfare Program is doing foundational research, including work on urban animals, and outreach. NYU’s WILD Lab is an applied research and outreach initiative dedicated to advancing the welfare of wild animals in urban environments. Their reports, Wild Animal Welfare in Local Policies on Human-Wildlife Conflict and Wild Animal Welfare in Local Policies on Land Use and the Built Environment, deal with city management from an urban welfare perspective.
  • PAZ, a French non-profit for animals, has a co-existing with liminal animals campaign 
  • Single-issue specialists: Preventing Bird-Building Collisions across Canada, Eurogroup for animals guide to animal-friendly management of urban pigeon populations
  • Urban wildlife organizations: Urban Wildlife Alliance (a grassroots, all volunteer organization dedicated to the welfare of NYC's wildlife), and research networks like UWIN. These are mostly framed as coexistence or conservation, putting less emphasis on individual welfare

Tractability

My intuition is that the influence activists can have on municipalities, and their ability to create change within the urban environments where they live, is greater than their ability to change the wild or even factory farming. In the city people actually come into contact with these animals and can help them personally, and many interventions can be a win-win for human and non-human animals. But this is just intuition, and a much deeper dive is needed, including interviews with activists who try to promote concrete interventions.

Examples of Interventions

My assumption is that most cost-effective interventions haven't been thought of yet, since the space is neglected. Nevertheless here are a few known interventions:

  • Rat contraceptive bait instead of poisoning. Its efficacy is still debated. Banning second-generation anticoagulant rodenticides is a possible ask.
  • Bird-safe glass legislation: this EA forum post, "If wild animal welfare is intractable, everything is intractable", mentions California's rodenticide ban and bird-safe-glass rules already passed in ~22 US cities. But the story is much more complicated, see reasons against this idea section.
  • Place cat food higher to protect hedgehogs: Hedgehogs suffer from a severe form of scabies. One possible reason is that cat food left on the street attracts hedgehogs, bringing them into repeated contact at the same feeding spots. A simple fix is to place the cats’ food higher, where cats can reach it but hedgehogs cannot. Anyone who has seen a hedgehog with advanced scabies knows how awful it can be. Their bodies can become covered in thick crusts, sometimes so badly that their eyes are not visible.
  • Swap steady red tower lights for blinking ones. On the ~4,500 tallest towers (over 150 m) in the United States and Canada, which cause most of the deaths, this could cut kills by ~45%, about 2.5 million birds a year (phys.org; Longcore et al. 2012, PLOS ONE)
  • A rainbow ruff collar on cats. Birds see the bright colors and flee. This intervention caused the killings of birds, reptiles and amphibians to drop ~54%, while cats still catch rats and mice (study summary).
  • Promote adoption of self driving car technologies to detect and avoid animals, including small animals near or under the vehicle. One Chinese self driving car demo already shows an underbody camera that can help avoid hitting animals while leaving a parking space. This new organization, Shared Roads, is working for "a multi-stakeholder approach to self-driving vehicle safety that accounts for every being on the road"

Scale

Urban animals:
I didn't find any global estimate of the number of urban vertebrates or invertebrates. My very initial estimate based on checking different AI estimates, which converge to similar numbers, is mostly extrapolation from some limited local data. It suggests there are 5-50 billion urban vertebrates at every moment, which is possibly more than factory farming (with about 30 billion at every moment). According to these estimates, urban animals are comprised of

  • a few billion, up to 10 billion birds
  • a few billion mice and rats
  • a few billion or less reptiles, amphibians and fish
  • ~ a billion free-roaming cats and dogs
  • other urban mammals (including bats), probably less than a billion

Hence, urban environments are dominated by small birds, rodents (mice and rats), reptiles and amphibians, which are the neglected majority. 

Confidence levels are low on those numbers. See the scale estimate for more details on these estimates.

55 percent of the world’s population, about 4.2 billion people, live in cities, and roughly seven in ten people are expected to live in urban areas by 2050 (UN DESA, World Urbanization Prospects). This means urban animal populations could grow as human designed environments expand at the expense of nature.

About 3% of earth's land is urban, but this number is expected to keep increasing.

Wild animals passing through:

  • In the US alone, building collisions kill over one billion birds annually. Extrapolated globally, this points to something on the order of ~25 billion bird collision deaths worldwide each year, though that is a very rough guess and the extrapolation is probably false
  • Roadkill: ~1 million vertebrates are killed every day in the US alone, according to an old study. Extrapolating from road network length (US ~6.6 million km versus ~64.3 million km worldwide (Wikipedia: road network size) gives roughly ~4 billion deaths a year, or about 2 billion according to another estimate on Wikipedia.
  • Vertebrates killed by urban cats amount to tens of billions globally each year: 1.3 to 4 billion birds and 6.3 to 22.3 billion mammals only in the US, but it's unclear how many of these deaths are due to urban cats.

Overall guesstimation: Billions or tens of billions of animals live in the urban environment every moment, and tens of billions more die every year passing through. This scale is big, though much smaller than wild animals, and seems in the general order of magnitude of land farmed animals .

My assumption is that a deep dive into this subject may increase the estimated scale.

Urban Insects

How many insects live in urban areas? Probably less than 2% of all earth's insects. It should be below the urban share of earth's land surface, which is 3%, because cities suppress insects. A global meta-analysis found urbanization cuts insect abundance by about 42% versus conserved land.

Even 1% of the estimated 10¹⁹ insects globally is about 10¹⁷ insects, 100 quadrillion individuals living in and around human settlements, on the order of 20 million insects per urban human.

If we could design and carry out any interventions for insects, or any education project about them, the city seems to me like the most plausible place to start.

Reasons in Favor of This Idea

What are the benefits of a nonprofit dedicated specifically to urban animal welfare, compared with programs run by organizations with a broader focus that work on animals both in nature and in cities? 

  • Although there may be many synergies between work on animals in nature and work on urban animals, as discussed in this section later on, cities are distinct environments with very different challenges. In urban environments, the main focus is reducing human-caused harms and designing cities that better accommodate the animals living in them
  • Urban animal advocacy avoids some of the philosophical difficulties involved in helping wild animals in nature. It could be much more consensual, and in many cases is aligned with direct human interests. I see no reason why urban animal advocacy can't become something pretty popular and not controversial
  • I think the urban animals branding, together with the points already mentioned, can attract more funding and people into working in this space, and more broadly into the animal advocacy movement, including a significant portion from outside the traditional farmed and wild animal movements. Most local urban animal activists are currently quite far, in my intuition, from EA and animal rights, but they are potential candidates to come much closer

The direct effects may be very substantial: 

  • Possibly roughly equal numbers of urban vertebrates and farmed land vertebrates may be alive at any given time
  • The urban landscape, where interventions can be more easily monitored, is like a simpler version of the more complicated fabric of life in nature
  • Helping urban animals directly helps humans (most people view reducing numbers of pigeons or mice, or fewer vehicle collisions with animals, as a good thing)
  • This space could potentially bring new money and people into the movement, not taking from existing resources (at least in the long run)
  • Mice, birds, and hedgehogs could be better served under one roof. 

The flow-through effects seem huge to me:

  • Urban animals can be a bridge for compassion to all the animals, because they are not behind closed doors or far away. People can get to know some of them personally, and their stories are easier to track and tell, no one is hiding them like with factory farmed animals. When individual stories of urban animals are told, human hearts are affected. Ruti the hyena is only one example.
  • Work on urban animals promotes thinking about a multispecies society
  • Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka's book Zoopolis (2011) argues for creatures who live among us (pigeons, rats, squirrels, raccoons) to gain the status of "denizens", residents of our societies. They can be a bridge for animal personhood.
  • Urban animals can serve as a bridge for sympathy with wild animals, as both groups are free and in need of help. They also blur the line between categories, since some animals live both in cities and in the wild, and wild animals often cross through urban areas.
  • Work on urban animals can help us understand how to reduce wild animal suffering, possibly creating pilot experiments for animal friendly designed environments. Animal friendly designed facilities, streets, and landscapes can serve as a living example of a welfare space for all.
  • Some specific technologies to help urban animals, such as non-surgical contraception, can also help wild animals (and may be easier to push for in cities, where they help humans too, than in the wild).
  • The city could be a place to build a connection between humans and insects? Highly speculative. Also see urban insects section

Reasons Against This Idea

  • The scale is big but not huge like with wild animal suffering or potentially digital suffering
  • Some organizations are already working on it, mostly at the local level
  • Wild animal welfare organizations are already carrying out some interventions for urban animals. There may be no need to add another category and a dedicated organization when this field already falls under wild animal welfare, specifically urban wildlife. I think otherwise, and in the previous section have explained why
  • Urban animal welfare wants to protect predators like mice that may kill many other animals, so total expected value from interventions could be unclear (albeit interventions for mice can also reduce their numbers). The urban area is simpler than the wild, but it's still very complicated. The post "Bird-safe glass may impact arthropods much more than birds?" raises concerns about the overall welfare footprint of the bird-safe glass intervention
  • The line between urban animals and wild animals is not always clear, as many animals live across both wild and urban environments

What the Nonprofit Could Do

Here are some possibilities:

  • Research and accumulation of all the worldwide knowledge about improving life for the urban multi-species society
    • Here are some research ideas:
      • How many urban animals are there worldwide? Existing research, such as Rethink Priorities’ abundance estimates for three relevant populations, could help answer this question. How many are vertebrates, how many are invertebrates, and, specifically, how many are insects?
      • What are the main causes of suffering for urban animals, and how do they compare to wild animal suffering from natural causes?
      • How many animals worldwide die from direct vehicle collisions, why does this happen, and which species are most affected? Answering these questions could help shape future regulation of autonomous vehicles and push the self-driving car industry toward technologies that better detect and avoid animals
      • The creation of human environments at the expense of wild ones: does it reduce the number of beings on earth? By how much?
      • Mapping different optional interventions and existing evidence for their effectiveness
  • Pilot interventions (based on the research) and helping local groups
  • Promoting the academic space of urban animal welfare, similar to how Wild Animal Initiative is promoting the academic space for welfare biology. This space is not the same as urban ecology
  • Bringing together experts from different fields to think about how to help urban animals, and supporting professional networks, such as Architects for Animals, that seek to help animals
    • The architect Dan Hasson argues that animals are the blind spot, the lacuna, of the architecture field. “Architecture is supposedly a humanistic discipline, but it revolves only around human beings. This practice does not see animals and does not think about them, even though planned spaces always affect animals as well. Animals are supposedly irrelevant" (source is in Hebrew)

Open Strategic Questions

  • How much emphasis should be put on promoting the academic study of multispecies urban welfare?
  • How much emphasis should be put on new technology vs working with existing tech?
  • What campaigns and coalitions for specific interventions can be very cost effective?
  • Is the main goal to improve urban animals' welfare (better lives) or to change their numbers (fewer of them, especially those that die very young)?

Conclusion

Urban animals, beyond cats and dogs, seem to be highly neglected, despite the problem’s large scale and potentially high tractability. Although there is uncertainty about the numbers, the interventions, and their overall impact, urban animal work has the potential to serve as a bridge toward caring about all sentient beings, help wild animals, and bring new funding and people into the field. This makes creating a global nonprofit for urban animals seem to me like a highly effective intervention.

You can read more of my thoughts about urban animals on my website, The Alien Journalist. The main arguments are all in this post, but the website adds some color.

Urban animals, sometimes described as liminal animals, are free animals living in human dominated environments, like pigeons, mice, lizards, hedgehogs, cats, insects and so on. The space of urban animal welfare can also include wild animals passing through urban areas, e.g. migrating birds, or animals living alternately between the urban and the wild, like jackals and boars.

Urban animals sit in the middle of the human domination spectrum; they are not confined like farmed animals, but not living in an evolutionarily designed environment like wild animals. They live in an environment very accurately crafted, but not for them😔. Humanity doesn't recognize that we live in a multi-species society, hence animals' interests are a neglected or nonexistent part of city planning, infrastructure, and architecture.

What do Urban Animals Suffer From? 

If we think about stray cats, most of them die very young, starve to death, suffer from disease, get hit by cars, lack safe spaces from heat and cold, and more. The infrastructure in the city, the food leftovers, and human behavior are not tuned to their welfare. The same causes of suffering (with some exceptions) also apply to pigeons, mice, rats, lizards and many other urban animals. Like wild animals, most urban animals don't have any "services" to help them; they are akin to living in a collapsed state, with no social or security services. 

Some examples: 
Like urban cats, most pigeons are born into short, fragile lives: in one urban colony study, roughly 45% of baby pigeons died within their first month after leaving the nest (Hetmański 2007), with the main cause of death being hunger. In some cases there are surprisingly easy solutions for reducing the suffering of urban animals, like egg swapping, replacing eggs with dummies to reduce pigeon reproduction.

The urban environment is a dangerous place for animals, and poisoning is one such danger: Rethink Priorities estimates, with high uncertainty, that about 31 million rodents in U.S. urban areas are exposed to rodenticides each year, and rodenticide poisoning can cause days of intense suffering before death.

Animals passing through the city can also be helped; more than a billion birds, many of whom are migrating, die annually in the US alone from building collisions, and terrestrial wild animals get hit by cars.

Neglectedness

Urban animals seem like an effective group to work on from a macro perspective because they are very neglected (not including cats and dogs). The space doesn't even have a clear well recognized name. Animals like mice, pigeons and reptiles living in urban areas are especially overlooked. A globally minded non-profit that tries to systematically change their lives on a macro scale, combining knowledge from experts in architecture, biology, and politics, is nowhere to be found, as far as I know.

Even for cats and dogs, for whom local initiatives are numerous, I didn't find an effective macro level organization that tries to tackle systematic issues, e.g. a technical solution to prevent cats from entering the engines of cars.

Most neglected is the global, cross city, evidence first layer. Existing urban animal work is often local, fragmented, emergency driven, or species siloed. There is activity, but it is usually focused on cats and dogs and not on systematic solutions.

Organizations Whose Work Includes Neglected Urban Animal Species

  • Wild Animal Initiative funds many urban animal welfare research projects. This list includes more than 80 research projects it has funded, many of which relate to urban animals and show that the line between urban animals and wild animals is not always clear
  • The Center for Wild Animal Welfare works to help wild animals, including those in urban areas, by promoting bird safe glass, fertility control (instead of painful poisons) for mice and rats, and much more
  • Sentience, "invisible animals" campaign. An effective-altruism-style push focused specifically on urban pigeons and rats, demanding humane pigeon lofts and a rodenticide phase-out (see related EA Forum post on interventions to improve pigeons’ welfare)
  • The NYU Wild Animal Welfare Program is doing foundational research, including work on urban animals, and outreach. NYU’s WILD Lab is an applied research and outreach initiative dedicated to advancing the welfare of wild animals in urban environments. Their reports, Wild Animal Welfare in Local Policies on Human-Wildlife Conflict and Wild Animal Welfare in Local Policies on Land Use and the Built Environment, deal with city management from an urban welfare perspective.
  • PAZ, a French non-profit for animals, has a co-existing with liminal animals campaign 
  • Single-issue specialists: Preventing Bird-Building Collisions across Canada, Eurogroup for animals guide to animal-friendly management of urban pigeon populations
  • Urban wildlife organizations: Urban Wildlife Alliance (a grassroots, all volunteer organization dedicated to the welfare of NYC's wildlife), and research networks like UWIN. These are mostly framed as coexistence or conservation, putting less emphasis on individual welfare

Tractability

My intuition is that the influence activists can have on municipalities, and their ability to create change within the urban environments where they live, is greater than their ability to change the wild or even factory farming. In the city people actually come into contact with these animals and can help them personally, and many interventions can be a win-win for human and non-human animals. But this is just intuition, and a much deeper dive is needed, including interviews with activists who try to promote concrete interventions.

Examples of Interventions

My assumption is that most cost-effective interventions haven't been thought of yet, since the space is neglected. Nevertheless here are a few known interventions:

  • Rat contraceptive bait instead of poisoning. Its efficacy is still debated. Banning second-generation anticoagulant rodenticides is a possible ask.
  • Bird-safe glass legislation: this EA forum post, "If wild animal welfare is intractable, everything is intractable", mentions California's rodenticide ban and bird-safe-glass rules already passed in ~22 US cities. But the story is much more complicated, see reasons against this idea section.
  • Place cat food higher to protect hedgehogs: Hedgehogs suffer from a severe form of scabies. One possible reason is that cat food left on the street attracts hedgehogs, bringing them into repeated contact at the same feeding spots. A simple fix is to place the cats’ food higher, where cats can reach it but hedgehogs cannot. Anyone who has seen a hedgehog with advanced scabies knows how awful it can be. Their bodies can become covered in thick crusts, sometimes so badly that their eyes are not visible.
  • Swap steady red tower lights for blinking ones. On the ~4,500 tallest towers (over 150 m) in the United States and Canada, which cause most of the deaths, this could cut kills by ~45%, about 2.5 million birds a year (phys.org; Longcore et al. 2012, PLOS ONE)
  • A rainbow ruff collar on cats. Birds see the bright colors and flee. This intervention caused the killings of birds, reptiles and amphibians to drop ~54%, while cats still catch rats and mice (study summary).
  • Promote adoption of self driving car technologies to detect and avoid animals, including small animals near or under the vehicle. One Chinese self driving car demo already shows an underbody camera that can help avoid hitting animals while leaving a parking space. This new organization, Shared Roads, is working for "a multi-stakeholder approach to self-driving vehicle safety that accounts for every being on the road"

Scale

Urban animals:
I didn't find any global estimate of the number of urban vertebrates or invertebrates. My very initial estimate based on checking different AI estimates, which converge to similar numbers, is mostly extrapolation from some limited local data. It suggests there are 5-50 billion urban vertebrates at every moment, which is possibly more than factory farming (with about 30 billion at every moment). According to these estimates, urban animals are comprised of

  • a few billion, up to 10 billion birds
  • a few billion mice and rats
  • a few billion or less reptiles, amphibians and fish
  • ~ a billion free-roaming cats and dogs
  • other urban mammals (including bats), probably less than a billion

Hence, urban environments are dominated by small birds, rodents (mice and rats), reptiles and amphibians, which are the neglected majority. 

Confidence levels are low on those numbers. See the scale estimate for more details on these estimates.

55 percent of the world’s population, about 4.2 billion people, live in cities, and roughly seven in ten people are expected to live in urban areas by 2050 (UN DESA, World Urbanization Prospects). This means urban animal populations could grow as human designed environments expand at the expense of nature.

About 3% of earth's land is urban, but this number is expected to keep increasing.

Wild animals passing through:

  • In the US alone, building collisions kill over one billion birds annually. Extrapolated globally, this points to something on the order of ~25 billion bird collision deaths worldwide each year, though that is a very rough guess and the extrapolation is probably false
  • Roadkill: ~1 million vertebrates are killed every day in the US alone, according to an old study. Extrapolating from road network length (US ~6.6 million km versus ~64.3 million km worldwide (Wikipedia: road network size) gives roughly ~4 billion deaths a year, or about 2 billion according to another estimate on Wikipedia.
  • Vertebrates killed by urban cats amount to tens of billions globally each year: 1.3 to 4 billion birds and 6.3 to 22.3 billion mammals only in the US, but it's unclear how many of these deaths are due to urban cats.

Overall guesstimation: Billions or tens of billions of animals live in the urban environment every moment, and tens of billions more die every year passing through. This scale is big, though much smaller than wild animals, and seems in the general order of magnitude of land farmed animals .

My assumption is that a deep dive into this subject may increase the estimated scale.

Urban Insects

How many insects live in urban areas? Probably less than 2% of all earth's insects. It should be below the urban share of earth's land surface, which is 3%, because cities suppress insects. A global meta-analysis found urbanization cuts insect abundance by about 42% versus conserved land.

Even 1% of the estimated 10¹⁹ insects globally is about 10¹⁷ insects, 100 quadrillion individuals living in and around human settlements, on the order of 20 million insects per urban human.

If we could design and carry out any interventions for insects, or any education project about them, the city seems to me like the most plausible place to start.

Reasons in Favor of This Idea

What are the benefits of a nonprofit dedicated specifically to urban animal welfare, compared with programs run by organizations with a broader focus that work on animals both in nature and in cities? 

  • Although there may be many synergies between work on animals in nature and work on urban animals, as discussed in this section later on, cities are distinct environments with very different challenges. In urban environments, the main focus is reducing human-caused harms and designing cities that better accommodate the animals living in them
  • Urban animal advocacy avoids some of the philosophical difficulties involved in helping wild animals in nature. It could be much more consensual, and in many cases is aligned with direct human interests. I see no reason why urban animal advocacy can't become something pretty popular and not controversial
  • I think the urban animals branding, together with the points already mentioned, can attract more funding and people into working in this space, and more broadly into the animal advocacy movement, including a significant portion from outside the traditional farmed and wild animal movements. Most local urban animal activists are currently quite far, in my intuition, from EA and animal rights, but they are potential candidates to come much closer

The direct effects may be very substantial: 

  • Possibly roughly equal numbers of urban vertebrates and farmed land vertebrates may be alive at any given time
  • The urban landscape, where interventions can be more easily monitored, is like a simpler version of the more complicated fabric of life in nature
  • Helping urban animals directly helps humans (most people view reducing numbers of pigeons or mice, or fewer vehicle collisions with animals, as a good thing)
  • This space could potentially bring new money and people into the movement, not taking from existing resources (at least in the long run)
  • Mice, birds, and hedgehogs could be better served under one roof. 

The flow-through effects seem huge to me:

  • Urban animals can be a bridge for compassion to all the animals, because they are not behind closed doors or far away. People can get to know some of them personally, and their stories are easier to track and tell, no one is hiding them like with factory farmed animals. When individual stories of urban animals are told, human hearts are affected. Ruti the hyena is only one example.
  • Work on urban animals promotes thinking about a multispecies society
  • Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka's book Zoopolis (2011) argues for creatures who live among us (pigeons, rats, squirrels, raccoons) to gain the status of "denizens", residents of our societies. They can be a bridge for animal personhood.
  • Urban animals can serve as a bridge for sympathy with wild animals, as both groups are free and in need of help. They also blur the line between categories, since some animals live both in cities and in the wild, and wild animals often cross through urban areas.
  • Work on urban animals can help us understand how to reduce wild animal suffering, possibly creating pilot experiments for animal friendly designed environments. Animal friendly designed facilities, streets, and landscapes can serve as a living example of a welfare space for all.
  • Some specific technologies to help urban animals, such as non-surgical contraception, can also help wild animals (and may be easier to push for in cities, where they help humans too, than in the wild).
  • The city could be a place to build a connection between humans and insects? Highly speculative. Also see urban insects section

Reasons Against This Idea

  • The scale is big but not huge like with wild animal suffering or potentially digital suffering
  • Some organizations are already working on it, mostly at the local level
  • Wild animal welfare organizations are already carrying out some interventions for urban animals. There may be no need to add another category and a dedicated organization when this field already falls under wild animal welfare, specifically urban wildlife. I think otherwise, and in the previous section have explained why
  • Urban animal welfare wants to protect predators like mice that may kill many other animals, so total expected value from interventions could be unclear (albeit interventions for mice can also reduce their numbers). The urban area is simpler than the wild, but it's still very complicated. The post "Bird-safe glass may impact arthropods much more than birds?" raises concerns about the overall welfare footprint of the bird-safe glass intervention
  • The line between urban animals and wild animals is not always clear, as many animals live across both wild and urban environments

What the Nonprofit Could Do

Here are some possibilities:

  • Research and accumulation of all the worldwide knowledge about improving life for the urban multi-species society
    • Here are some research ideas:
      • How many urban animals are there worldwide? Existing research, such as Rethink Priorities’ abundance estimates for three relevant populations, could help answer this question. How many are vertebrates, how many are invertebrates, and, specifically, how many are insects?
      • What are the main causes of suffering for urban animals, and how do they compare to wild animal suffering from natural causes?
      • How many animals worldwide die from direct vehicle collisions, why does this happen, and which species are most affected? Answering these questions could help shape future regulation of autonomous vehicles and push the self-driving car industry toward technologies that better detect and avoid animals
      • The creation of human environments at the expense of wild ones: does it reduce the number of beings on earth? By how much?
      • Mapping different optional interventions and existing evidence for their effectiveness
  • Pilot interventions (based on the research) and helping local groups
  • Promoting the academic space of urban animal welfare, similar to how Wild Animal Initiative is promoting the academic space for welfare biology. This space is not the same as urban ecology
  • Bringing together experts from different fields to think about how to help urban animals, and supporting professional networks, such as Architects for Animals, that seek to help animals
    • The architect Dan Hasson argues that animals are the blind spot, the lacuna, of the architecture field. “Architecture is supposedly a humanistic discipline, but it revolves only around human beings. This practice does not see animals and does not think about them, even though planned spaces always affect animals as well. Animals are supposedly irrelevant" (source is in Hebrew)

Open Strategic Questions

  • How much emphasis should be put on promoting the academic study of multispecies urban welfare?
  • How much emphasis should be put on new technology vs working with existing tech?
  • What campaigns and coalitions for specific interventions can be very cost effective?
  • Is the main goal to improve urban animals' welfare (better lives) or to change their numbers (fewer of them, especially those that die very young)?

Conclusion

Urban animals, beyond cats and dogs, seem to be highly neglected, despite the problem’s large scale and potentially high tractability. Although there is uncertainty about the numbers, the interventions, and their overall impact, urban animal work has the potential to serve as a bridge toward caring about all sentient beings, help wild animals, and bring new funding and people into the field. This makes creating a global nonprofit for urban animals seem to me like a highly effective intervention.

You can read more of my thoughts about urban animals on my website, The Alien Journalist. The main arguments are all in this post, but the website adds some color.

item.title: AIM’s new approach to incubating for the animals (applications open!)
item.description:
Published on August 3, 2026 2:51 PM GMT

TL;DR: Applications are open for AIM's first ever animal-only incubation round. The program runs February 2027, and it is different from any round we've run before: we’ve rebuilt the research process with animal welfare in mind, recommending frontier problems rather than fully-scoped solutions, there is a new funded three-month exploration phase after the core program, and two weeks in San Francisco alongside the movement's biggest funders and thinkers. Aaron Boddy (co-founder of Shrimp Welfare Project) has joined to help design and run it. Applications close 13th September.

--

A few months ago, we wrote about why now might be the best time ever to start an animal charity. In short: the bottlenecks that limited us to incubating roughly two to four animal charities a year are easing on both sides, us finding more superstar founders excited to work on animal welfare and mid-stage funding becoming less of a limiting factor than it was a few years ago. Meanwhile, the animal movement needs more new interventions and organizations in the pipeline so that efforts to fix factory farming can scale in the coming years. The low-hanging fruit hasn't been picked because barely anyone is in the orchard: Incubating more trailblazing animal charities is one way to help address this.

That post explained why we're running a dedicated animal round. This post explains what’s different about it.

What's different about this round

1. Everything is pointed at animals. Our incubation program was built to accommodate a wide range of charity types, and we've long hypothesised that more focused rounds, where the approach is tailored to a specific type of charity’s needs, will increase our hit-rate of field-leading organizations. This round we put that hypothesis to the test: Our research process, our recruitment priorities, the program structure and curriculum, the program managers and the mentors are all being rebuilt around what animal charities specifically need rather than what works on average across cause areas.

2. We're recommending frontier problems, not fully-scoped solutions. Historically our research team handed founders a specified intervention to implement. This round, mostly, we won't. (More on this below).

3. Three funded months to explore. Because we're recommending problems rather than fully-scoped solutions, you won't submit a seed funding proposal at the end of the eight weeks. Instead you’ll submit an “exploration plan” for how you'll immerse yourself in the stakeholder and industry landscape, and design and test candidate theories of change before choosing what to pilot. Stipends will continue throughout the three-month exploration phase, plus a dedicated grant to cover the costs involved (e.g. flights, contractors, materials). And if you already know what you want to build and scale, you don't have to wait — you can submit for seed funding whenever you're ready. The exploration phase is there to provide you the freedom to explore rather than having to submit a premature funding proposal bears little resemblance to your eventual plan and budget needs.

4. Time in San Francisco. As always, the program includes 2 mandatory weeks at the AIM office in London to spend time with your cohort and to immerse yourself in our community of entrepreneurs. But this time, that will be followed by several weeks in San Francisco, optional but strongly recommended, timed to overlap with EAG Bay Area and the Sentient Futures Summit. The point is (1) to test your early thinking on the movement’s thought leaders while it's still cheap to change your mind, and (2) to inspire you to think bigger. All expenses paid, visa support/advice available for your travel to the UK and US.

5. Aaron Boddy is helping run it. Aaron co-founded Shrimp Welfare Project through our program in 2021, having previously not thought much about shrimp at all. Today, SWP provides electrical stunners to dozens of shrimp producers in 9 countries, serving 11 retailers. They estimate that their work currently causes 6.5 billion shrimps per year to experience less suffering at the end of their lives. He has done the thing we're asking founders to do in this next round: explore a neglected problem on the frontier of the animal movement and find and scale new solutions to help them by the billion.

6. Meeting a wider range of financial needs. It's important to us that meeting financial needs isn't a blocker to the best talent founding a charity. Our goal has always been to cover the program’s costs and provide stipends so program participants can focus on founding a charity. In practice, our guidelines and norms about these stipends and about founder salaries after the program have made it difficult for people higher financial needs to choose the charity founder path. To this end, we’re overhauling our stipend policy and founder salary guidance: We will actively encourage those with higher financial needs to request higher stipends, and we are committed to accommodating those requests where reasonable. Meanwhile we will continue to encourage people with lower needs (no dependents, low cost-of-living location) to ask for less so the difference goes to beneficiaries. We have an entire post on changes to AIM’s stipend and salary post coming next week.

7. Bigger ambition. We've incubated field-leading farmed animal charities before, including two that have been recommended by ACE. Given that we know this is possible and that impact is power-lawed, we are focusing all our effort on creating more field leaders. This means we’re not interested in incubating charities that, if successful, will merely inch the movement's current trajectory forward. We want charities that shift what the movement thinks is possible.

More on “frontier problems”

Relative to causes like global health, animal welfare has far fewer well-evidenced, fully-scoped interventions that aren't already being pursued extensively by existing actors. But the good news is that it has plenty of big problems that are eminently solvable and have strong willingness to pay from funders, industry or consumers to solve them. So the founder's job becomes exploring the problem space and figuring out how to remove the pain point.

This is fairly typical of how for-profit founders and funders think: Knowing the exact solution from the outset matters less than finding a large-scale pain point with high willingness to pay. Backing talented founders with the resources to explore and test solutions makes for a winning investment.

We believe this change will be very exciting for some and very intimidating for others. 

  • Historically, because we’ve recommended relatively fully-scoped interventions, our applicants have naturally skewed towards people who find this attractive. These folks may find the more open-ended exploration process intimidating. To them we say: worry not! We will still plan to recommend some relatively fully-scoped solutions, as we have always done, so apply now!
  • On the other hand, we suspect there is a large set of would-be superstar founders who have not applied to our program because they see exploring and finding a solution themselves as the most exciting part of entrepreneurship. To them we say: this program is perfect for you, so apply now!

The research process

Right now our research team is busy sourcing and assessing over 100 problems at the frontier of the movement and narrowing them to a recommended shortlist. We’ll be assessing each problem on factors like:

  • The scale of potential addressable impact
  • The economics and how conducive they are to cost-effective interventions
  • The strength of the underlying evidence
  • The stakeholder landscape (to what extent are there supportive actors / is the opposition surmountable / is the market formal / is regulation enforced?)
  • Whether we can already see several plausible solutions worth testing

Illustrative examples we're excited about

We’re far from locking in any recommendations, but what we can do is share some big picture categories that we're excited about, going into the process. We won't necessarily recommend frontier problems in all of these categories, and we'll almost certainly recommend others. (Naturally, we’ll coordinate with the various other incubators working on animal welfare so that we play to our comparative advantages.)

Welfare tech

i.e. Developing new welfare technology, driving producer adoption of existing technology, or acting as an evaluator or certifier.

  • Why it matters: technology can deliver welfare gains at scale without depending on sustained consumer behaviour change, which is extremely hard to achieve.
  • Example: bringing in-ovo sexing to major Asian egg producers. The technology to sex embryos before hatch already exists and is being adopted in Europe following chick-culling bans, but the world's largest egg-producing regions still cull day-old male chicks by the billion.

Enabling primary animal welfare research. 

i.e. Getting more, better and faster actionable research produced, for instance by re-granting to academics with milestone-gated funding that pushes on timelines, methodology and relevance to implementers.[1] 

  • Why it matters: many solutions can't yet be designed or evaluated because the underlying science on what actually matters for different species' welfare is underdeveloped.
  • Example: commissioning research to identify which changes to farming practices would most improve juvenile fish welfare, so corporate and funder resources target the highest-impact reforms.

Talent meta-charities. 

i.e. Moving new talent into the movement, helping organisations absorb it through management and onboarding support, or upskilling the people already here.

  • Why it matters: senior judgment and management capacity, not money, is often the binding constraint on the movement's growth.
  • Example: a structured fellowship placing experienced industry operators into animal orgs, or management training built specifically for animal welfare leaders.

Neglected animal populations. 

i.e. Crowding resources into a high-scale, low-attention population the way Shrimp Welfare Project did for farmed shrimp, and LEEP did for lead.

  • Why it matters: some of the largest sources of animal suffering are also the most ignored. The first actor in gets to pick the lowest-hanging fruit and blaze a trail for others..
  • Example: a welfare organisation for honeybees.

You don't need to be an "animal person"

The previous post covers this at length, so briefly: you don't need to be vegan, you don't need an animal-movement background, and you don't need to feel much when you see a chicken. You need to take seriously that factory farming is one of the biggest problems of our time, and be willing to follow the evidence on what will fix it.

Key dates and how to apply

The animal round

  • Applications close 13th September. Apply here.
  • Offers go out in December. Book club in January. Core program 1st February to 5th April 2027, followed by the three-month exploration phase and seed funding from July.
  • Webinars (sign up):
    • 26th August with Steve Thompson on how the program works and how to tell if you're a good fit.
    • 2nd September with Aaron Boddy on exploring frontier problems.
    • 9th September with Emma Stoks on the application and selection process.
  • More detail on the program page.

But what about other cause areas? 

We will be incubating charities working on health system strengthening, livelihoods and economic growth in H2 2027. You can apply for that program now as well (and there will be another opportunity to do so early next year).

Thanks for reading!

  1. ^

     It may also include enabling more and better monitoring and evaluation of existing animal welfare work, so we can identify and scale what’s working faster.

This means we’re not interested in incubating charities that, if successful, will merely inch the movement's current trajectory forward. We want charities that shift what the movement thinks is possible.

More on “frontier problems”

Relative to causes like global health, animal welfare has far fewer well-evidenced, fully-scoped interventions that aren't already being pursued extensively by existing actors. But the good news is that it has plenty of big problems that are eminently solvable and have strong willingness to pay from funders, industry or consumers to solve them. So the founder's job becomes exploring the problem space and figuring out how to remove the pain point.

This is fairly typical of how for-profit founders and funders think: Knowing the exact solution from the outset matters less than finding a large-scale pain point with high willingness to pay. Backing talented founders with the resources to explore and test solutions makes for a winning investment.

We believe this change will be very exciting for some and very intimidating for others. 

  • Historically, because we’ve recommended relatively fully-scoped interventions, our applicants have naturally skewed towards people who find this attractive. These folks may find the more open-ended exploration process intimidating. To them we say: worry not! We will still plan to recommend some relatively fully-scoped solutions, as we have always done, so apply now!
  • On the other hand, we suspect there is a large set of would-be superstar founders who have not applied to our program because they see exploring and finding a solution themselves as the most exciting part of entrepreneurship. To them we say: this program is perfect for you, so apply now!

The research process

Right now our research team is busy sourcing and assessing over 100 problems at the frontier of the movement and narrowing them to a recommended shortlist. We’ll be assessing each problem on factors like:

  • The scale of potential addressable impact
  • The economics and how conducive they are to cost-effective interventions
  • The strength of the underlying evidence
  • The stakeholder landscape (to what extent are there supportive actors / is the opposition surmountable / is the market formal / is regulation enforced?)
  • Whether we can already see several plausible solutions worth testing

Illustrative examples we're excited about

We’re far from locking in any recommendations, but what we can do is share some big picture categories that we're excited about, going into the process. We won't necessarily recommend frontier problems in all of these categories, and we'll almost certainly recommend others. (Naturally, we’ll coordinate with the various other incubators working on animal welfare so that we play to our comparative advantages.)

Welfare tech

i.e. Developing new welfare technology, driving producer adoption of existing technology, or acting as an evaluator or certifier.

  • Why it matters: technology can deliver welfare gains at scale without depending on sustained consumer behaviour change, which is extremely hard to achieve.
  • Example: bringing in-ovo sexing to major Asian egg producers. The technology to sex embryos before hatch already exists and is being adopted in Europe following chick-culling bans, but the world's largest egg-producing regions still cull day-old male chicks by the billion.

Enabling primary animal welfare research. 

i.e. Getting more, better and faster actionable research produced, for instance by re-granting to academics with milestone-gated funding that pushes on timelines, methodology and relevance to implementers.[1] 

  • Why it matters: many solutions can't yet be designed or evaluated because the underlying science on what actually matters for different species' welfare is underdeveloped.
  • Example: commissioning research to identify which changes to farming practices would most improve juvenile fish welfare, so corporate and funder resources target the highest-impact reforms.

Talent meta-charities. 

i.e. Moving new talent into the movement, helping organisations absorb it through management and onboarding support, or upskilling the people already here.

  • Why it matters: senior judgment and management capacity, not money, is often the binding constraint on the movement's growth.
  • Example: a structured fellowship placing experienced industry operators into animal orgs, or management training built specifically for animal welfare leaders.

Neglected animal populations. 

i.e. Crowding resources into a high-scale, low-attention population the way Shrimp Welfare Project did for farmed shrimp, and LEEP did for lead.

  • Why it matters: some of the largest sources of animal suffering are also the most ignored. The first actor in gets to pick the lowest-hanging fruit and blaze a trail for others..
  • Example: a welfare organisation for honeybees.

You don't need to be an "animal person"

The previous post covers this at length, so briefly: you don't need to be vegan, you don't need an animal-movement background, and you don't need to feel much when you see a chicken. You need to take seriously that factory farming is one of the biggest problems of our time, and be willing to follow the evidence on what will fix it.

Key dates and how to apply

The animal round

  • Applications close 13th September. Apply here.
  • Offers go out in December. Book club in January. Core program 1st February to 5th April 2027, followed by the three-month exploration phase and seed funding from July.
  • Webinars (sign up):
    • 26th August with Steve Thompson on how the program works and how to tell if you're a good fit.
    • 2nd September with Aaron Boddy on exploring frontier problems.
    • 9th September with Emma Stoks on the application and selection process.
  • More detail on the program page.

But what about other cause areas? 

We will be incubating charities working on health system strengthening, livelihoods and economic growth in H2 2027. You can apply for that program now as well (and there will be another opportunity to do so early next year).

Thanks for reading!

  1. ^

     It may also include enabling more and better monitoring and evaluation of existing animal welfare work, so we can identify and scale what’s working faster.
